ASTRA: Personal Health Baselines for Long-Duration Spaceflight
overview : ASTRA is a browser-based prototype for personalized astronaut health monitoring. Spaceflight conditions such as microgravity, disrupted sleep, and changing workloads can influence health measurements. general reference values may not capture each astronaut’s individual patterns.

The system monitors six indicators : heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose , body temperature, sleep duration, and mood. it compares new measurements with earlier records from the same astronaut, considering context such as activity, posture, meal timing , measurement method, and sleep schedule.

Its baseline engine calculates a personal historical median and the difference between that baseline and a new reading. It estimates individual variability using the Median absolute Deviation (MAD), and provides empirical percentiles, measurement quality filtering, and data confidence information. These outputs describe comparisons with personal history; they are not medical diagnoses or risk scores.

Users can enter hypothetical measurements and explore how results change with context and available mission history.

The prototype uses approximately 2,400 synthatic measurements from three fictional astronauts. Built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, it runs in a browser without a backend or paid APIs. It is not clinically validated, and its dataset does not represent real astronaut medical records as it is just a protoype.
details:
ASTRA: Context-Aware Personal Health Monitoring for Astronauts

ASTRA is a browser-based prototype designed to explore how astronauts' health measurements could be interpreted in the context of their own historical patterns during space missions.

Health measurements can vary with factors such as physical activity, posture, meal timing, sleep schedules and measurement conditions. A generalized reference range may not fully represent an individual's usual pattern. ASTRA addresses this challenge by comparing a new measurement with earlier observations from the same astronaut under comparable conditions.

The prototype currently supports six indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep duration and mood. For each indicator, it selects comparable historical records, applies data-quality filtering and calculates a personal historical median, scaled median absolute deviation (MAD) and empirical percentile. It also displays a data-confidence category based on the number of comparable observations available. This confidence category describes the depth of the historical sample, not medical risk or diagnostic certainty.

The application includes interactive historical visualizations and a hypothetical-measurement feature. Users can enter a hypothetical reading and select its context to explore how it compares with the astronaut's historical baseline. These entries are temporary and do not modify the original dataset.

The prototype uses approximately 2,400 synthetic records representing three fictional astronauts over an approximately 60-day mission. It does not use real astronaut medical records, live telemetry or connected medical sensors. The statistical approach is exploratory and has not been clinically validated.

Development and tools: The application was developed using HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript and deployed through Netlify. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with generating and revising website code. ChatGPT (OpenAI) assisted with code review, debugging guidance. AI tools were used transparently; I brainstormed the ideas, Improved the fascinating one, directed the project, reviewed the generated outputs, tested the application and handled its deployment.

The project's design was informed by research and resources concerning human spaceflight health monitoring, including NASA Human Research Program materials and NASA Standard Measures. Additional background resources from the Canadian Space Agency, TRISH and Axiom Space were also consulted.

The main design considerations were contextual comparability, transparent statistical interpretation, data quality, sample size, usability and the limitations of synthetic data. ASTRABASELINE is a research-oriented prototype, not a clinical decision-support or diagnostic system.
